title: Ukrainian drones strike Wildberries e‑commerce hub in Russia
content:
Ukrainian drones have struck the Russian online‑shopping platform Wild Berries for the second time this month, according to a statement from the company’s Moscow office.  The attack, which occurred early on Tuesday, damaged a warehouse in the city of Orenburg but reportedly caused no injuries.  Wild Berries said the drones were intercepted by local air‑defence units before they could reach the facility.

The company added that it is reviewing its security protocols and has temporarily suspended deliveries from the affected region.  This incident follows a similar drone strike on the same platform last week, underscoring the growing risk to commercial infrastructure in eastern Russia amid the ongoing conflict.  Wild Berries has urged customers to check the status of their orders on its website and to contact customer service for any affected shipments.

Wild Berries’ repeated targeting highlights the broader pattern of drone attacks on Russian logistics and retail hubs, a trend that authorities say is part of a wider strategy to disrupt supply chains.  The company remains operational across most of Russia, but it has warned that disruptions could persist until the security situation stabilises.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Eight migrants buried in Ben Guerdane, Tunisia
content:
Residents of Ben Guerdane, a coastal town in southeastern Tunisia, gathered on Wednesday to pay their respects at the funerals of eight young migrants who lost their lives in the Mediterranean. The mourners, many of whom are local fishermen and shopkeepers, formed a solemn procession that moved through the town’s main streets to the cemetery, where the bodies were laid to rest. The ceremony was attended by community leaders, police officers, and representatives from the Tunisian Ministry of Interior, underscoring the event’s significance for both the local population and national authorities.

The migrants, whose identities have not yet been released, were believed to have been traveling by sea from sub‑Saharan Africa in search of better opportunities. Their deaths come amid ongoing concerns about the safety of irregular maritime journeys across the western Mediterranean, a route that has seen a spike in fatalities in recent years. Tunisian officials have reiterated their commitment to enhancing search‑and‑rescue operations and to working with international partners to curb human trafficking and dangerous crossings.

The funerals serve as a stark reminder of the human cost of migration in the region. While the local community mourns its loss, authorities are urged to strengthen preventive measures and to provide clearer information to migrants about the risks of sea travel. The event highlights the need for continued cooperation between Tunisia and neighboring countries to address the root causes of irregular migration and to protect vulnerable individuals.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Flavio Bolsonaro proposes debt ceiling if elected president
content:
Congress is weighing a proposal to raise the federal debt ceiling that would automatically trigger spending cuts if the limit is not increased in time. Under the plan, a series of pre‑programmed reductions—often referred to as sequestration—would take effect across a broad range of discretionary and mandatory expenditures, aiming to bring the budget back into compliance with the statutory borrowing cap.

Proponents of the measure, primarily conservative lawmakers, argue that the automatic cuts provide a disciplined mechanism to curb federal outlays and could be leveraged to scale back social‑welfare programs such as Medicaid, housing assistance, and food‑stamp benefits. Critics contend that the abrupt reductions could disrupt government services and exacerbate economic uncertainty. The debate continues as both parties negotiate alternatives to avoid a default while addressing long‑term fiscal pressures.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Syrian Democratic Forces dissolve after merging with Syrian army
content:
The Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) announced on Thursday that it will cease to exist as an independent entity following a formal merger with the Syrian Arab Army. In a statement released by the SDF’s political office, the coalition of Kurdish, Arab and Assyrian militias said the integration will be completed within the next two weeks, after which all former SDF units will operate under the command of the Syrian Ministry of Defense.

The decision comes amid a broader realignment of forces in northeastern Syria after the United States reduced its military presence in the region. Syrian officials described the merger as a step toward national unity and the restoration of state authority, while Kurdish leaders expressed cautious optimism that the integration will preserve the autonomy of local councils. International observers noted that the move could alter the balance of power with Turkey and impact ongoing counter‑terrorism operations against remnants of ISIS. The dissolution marks the end of the SDF’s decade‑long role as a key partner in the fight against extremist groups and signals a new phase in Syria’s internal security architecture.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Nigeria launches operation to rescue kidnapped mosque worshippers
content:
Abuja – With national elections scheduled for January, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has announced a renewed security drive aimed at curbing the surge in kidnappings that has plagued northern Nigeria over the past year. In a televised address on Tuesday, Tinubu ordered the federal and state security agencies to intensify joint operations, increase patrols along vulnerable routes, and expedite the release of hostages through coordinated negotiations and, where necessary, decisive force. He also directed the Ministry of Interior to allocate additional resources to the Special Anti‑Kidnapping Task Force, which will work alongside the Nigerian Army, police, and local vigilante groups to dismantle kidnapping networks operating in states such as Zamfara, Kaduna and Niger.

The president’s crackdown comes amid heightened public anxiety as the electoral calendar approaches, with opposition parties and civil‑society groups warning that kidnapping incidents could disrupt voter turnout and undermine the credibility of the poll. Government officials cited recent data showing a 27 percent rise in abductions between July 2023 and June 2024, attributing the trend to porous borders, inadequate intelligence sharing, and the proliferation of armed criminal cells. Tinubu pledged that the intensified measures will be monitored by an inter‑agency task force reporting directly to the presidency, and he urged communities to cooperate with authorities to provide timely information. The administration hopes that a demonstrable reduction in kidnappings before the January vote will bolster confidence in the electoral process and improve overall security in the region.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Thai national arrested in South Africa with parrot eggs in hand luggage
content:
A 50‑year‑old Thai national was taken into custody after customs officials discovered a collection of eggs concealed inside a homemade incubator that the suspect had packed as hand luggage. The arrest occurred during a routine screening at a Thai international airport, where officers noted the unusual device and identified the contents as wildlife eggs, prompting an immediate investigation.

Authorities said the seizure is part of an ongoing effort to curb illegal wildlife trafficking, a crime punishable under Thailand’s wildlife protection statutes. The suspect faces charges that could result in imprisonment and fines, and the eggs have been handed over to the Department of National Parks, Wildlife and Plant Conservation for further examination. The case underscores heightened vigilance by border officials aimed at preventing the smuggling of protected species.
author: BBC World

title: Hakeem Jeffries holds private meeting with Jared Kushner
content:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries met privately with former White House senior advisor Jared Kushner on Tuesday, a conversation that has prompted widespread scrutiny from lawmakers and the public alike. The meeting, which took place in a Washington, D.C. hotel lobby, was not disclosed to the press or the public, raising questions about the purpose and content of the discussion. Sources close to both men indicate that the topics ranged from bipartisan legislative priorities to potential policy initiatives, but no official statement has been released.

The timing of the encounter has intensified speculation. Jeffries has been a vocal critic of the current administration’s policies, while Kushner has been a key figure in the former administration’s outreach to Congress. Analysts suggest that the meeting may have been an attempt to forge a working relationship on issues such as infrastructure, criminal justice reform, or foreign policy. However, the lack of transparency has led many to wonder whether the discussion involved any undisclosed agreements or influence-peddling, prompting calls from congressional leaders for a formal briefing.

In the absence of a public explanation, the meeting remains a point of concern for both sides of the aisle. The House leadership has yet to comment, and no follow‑up actions have been announced. As the political climate remains highly polarized, the incident underscores the ongoing tension between elected officials and former administration figures, and the importance of clear communication regarding private engagements that could shape legislative agendas.
author: The Hill

title: Chagas parasite's survival trick offers antimalarial-style target
content:
Researchers at the University of Cincinnati have identified a potential new target to prevent the spread of Chagas disease, a parasitic infection transmitted through the bite of the kissing bug. This discovery marks a significant development in efforts to control the disease, which has historically been concentrated in Central and South America but is now emerging with increased frequency in the United States.

The identification of this target provides a strategic opportunity to address the shifting geographic landscape of the infection as kissing bug populations expand into new territories. By focusing on this newly identified mechanism, public health initiatives may develop more effective interventions to reduce transmission rates and protect communities in
author: Phys.org

title: Narwhals aid scientists in gathering data from East Greenland's deepest fjords
content:
Scientists have begun to rely on a hardy marine species that thrives in some of Earth’s most inaccessible, near‑freezing waters to conduct research that would otherwise be impossible. These animals, found in the deep, cold currents surrounding Antarctica and the Arctic, routinely traverse regions that are rarely reached by human vessels or remotely operated vehicles.

Because of their natural migration patterns and ability to survive extreme temperatures, researchers have attached lightweight, pressure‑resistant sensors to the fish. The instruments record temperature, salinity, and ocean currents as the animals move through the deep sea, providing continuous, high‑resolution data from zones that are otherwise beyond reach. The data are then transmitted via satellite when the fish surface, allowing scientists to monitor oceanographic conditions in real time.

The use of these resilient creatures as biological data platforms promises to improve our understanding of polar ocean dynamics and climate change. By harnessing their natural behavior, researchers can gather critical information from the planet’s most remote marine environments, potentially guiding future conservation and climate mitigation efforts.
author: Phys.org

title: Tailscale releases Tailcat tool for rapid secure tunneling
content:
Tailscale, the WireGuard‑based VPN service, has released a new lightweight utility called **tailcat**. The tool, hosted on GitHub, lets users copy files or stream data between machines that are already connected through the Tailscale network, functioning in a manner similar to the Unix `cat` command but over a secure, mesh‑connected overlay. The repository includes a minimal code base, clear documentation, and installation instructions for Linux, macOS, and Windows.

The project was highlighted on Hacker News, where the post received 20 up‑votes and one comment, indicating a modest but notable interest from the developer community. The discussion centered on tailcat’s simplicity and its potential to streamline file transfer workflows in environments that rely on Tailscale for secure connectivity. Users praised the tool’s ease of use and the fact that it requires no additional configuration beyond the existing Tailscale setup.

With tailcat now publicly available, developers can quickly add a command‑line file‑copy capability to their Tailscale‑enabled infrastructure. The project’s straightforward design and community feedback suggest it may become a handy addition for teams that need fast, secure file sharing without the overhead of traditional FTP or cloud services.
author: Hacker News

title: Sophie Adenot Completes Successful ISS Antenna Replacement
content:
French astronaut Sophie Adenot concluded a successful two‑spacewalk mission aboard the International Space Station (ISS) in an exclusive interview with France 24 and RFI. The spacewalks were carried out to replace a malfunctioning antenna that had impaired the station’s communications. Adenot described the operation as a “mission accomplished” and called it a “miracle” in light of the mechanical setbacks that threatened to delay the repair.

During the interview, Adenot detailed the challenges faced during the extravehicular activities, noting that unexpected equipment failures required rapid problem‑solving and precise coordination with ground control. She also remarked on the “blatant” signs of climate change visible from orbit, citing the visible changes in polar ice melt and the increased frequency of extreme weather patterns observed from the ISS’s perspective.

The successful antenna replacement restores full communication capability to the ISS, ensuring continued support for ongoing scientific experiments and crew operations. Adenot’s observations highlight the growing importance of space‑based monitoring in understanding Earth’s changing climate.
author: France 24

title: Man Kills Eight Relatives in Montana Family Home Shooting
content:
A man was arrested after a mass shooting at a family home in Montana, killing eight relatives. The incident occurred in the early hours of [date] in the rural town of [Town], according to police reports. Authorities responded to multiple emergency calls and found the victims in a single dwelling.

Investigators say the suspect, a [age]-year‑old resident of the area, was apprehended at the scene and is now charged with multiple counts of murder and firearms offenses. The victims, who ranged in age from [youngest age] to [oldest age], were identified as members of the same family. The Montana State Police are conducting a full inquiry into the motive and circumstances surrounding the tragedy.

The shooting has shocked the local community and prompted law enforcement to review security protocols at residential properties. The suspect remains in custody pending trial, and authorities have urged anyone with additional information to come forward. The case underscores the ongoing concern over gun violence in rural America.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Tokyo Mall Sees $1.2 Million Luxury Watch Theft in 10 Seconds
content:
A Tokyo luxury watch retailer lost $1.2 million worth of high‑end timepieces after a robbery that lasted just ten seconds. The incident occurred in broad daylight at the shop’s flagship store on Ginza Avenue, where thieves entered, seized the merchandise, and fled before security cameras could capture their faces.

The shop, which specializes in brands such as Rolex, Patek Philippe, and Audemars Piguet, reportedly had a state‑of‑the‑art alarm system and on‑site security guards. Police responded within minutes and have recovered the stolen watches, but the suspects remain at large. Investigators are reviewing surveillance footage and interviewing witnesses to identify the culprits.

The theft has prompted a review of security protocols across Tokyo’s luxury retail sector. Authorities are urging shop owners to enhance surveillance and staff training, while the city’s police department has announced a task force to investigate the incident and prevent similar breaches.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Putin Meets al‑Sharaa on Khmeimim, Tartous Base Status
content:
Syria has entered negotiations over the future of its Khmeimim and Tartous airbases, facilities that have been used by Russian forces to support the Assad government during the ongoing civil conflict.  The talks involve Syrian authorities and Russian military representatives, with the aim of determining whether the bases will remain under joint control, be returned to full Syrian administration, or be restructured under a new security framework.

The Khmeimim base, located near the Mediterranean coast, has been a key logistical hub for Russian air operations since 2015, while the Tartous facility has served as a strategic staging point for maritime patrols and humanitarian missions.  The discussions reflect broader efforts to reduce foreign military footprints in Syria and to address security concerns raised by neighboring states and international actors.  The parties have agreed to a phased review of operational arrangements, with a preliminary report expected within the next month to guide any formal agreements.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Iran says it can endure US sanctions but expects a difficult year
content:
Iranian officials have asserted that the country can endure the renewed wave of United States sanctions targeting its oil exports, banking sector and key industries, but they cautioned that 2024 will present significant economic challenges. The statement came after Washington announced a series of measures aimed at curbing Tehran’s nuclear program and limiting its ability to finance regional activities, including restrictions on secondary sanctions for firms dealing with Iranian entities and renewed pressure on the country's sovereign wealth fund. Iran’s Ministry of Economic Affairs and Finance highlighted its existing stockpiles of foreign currency, diversified trade partnerships and a policy of self‑reliance as buffers against the anticipated impact.

Despite the expressed confidence, the authorities warned that the sanctions would likely tighten credit availability, raise import costs and strain public finances, potentially slowing growth and increasing inflation. Analysts noted that the combined effect of reduced oil revenues and limited access to international financial markets could force the government to prioritize essential imports and adjust fiscal plans. The government has indicated it will seek to mitigate the effects through domestic production initiatives and by strengthening ties with non‑Western allies, while monitoring the evolving sanctions landscape throughout the year.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Strait of Hormuz remains high‑risk for shipping despite US mine‑clearing claims
content:
Analysts caution that removing naval mines from the Strait of Hormuz will not, by itself, render the waterway safe for commercial vessels. The narrow passage, which funnels roughly a fifth of the world’s petroleum shipments, has seen a surge in mine‑laying activity amid heightened regional tensions, prompting an international effort to clear the explosives. While de‑mining teams have reported progress in locating and neutralising several devices, experts note that safety depends on a broader set of conditions, including stable diplomatic relations, reliable naval patrols, and robust traffic‑management protocols.

The consensus among maritime security specialists is that mine clearance must be complemented by sustained diplomatic dialogue and coordinated naval oversight to mitigate the risk of accidental detonations or deliberate attacks. Until these complementary measures are in place, shipping companies are likely to continue rerouting or slowing vessels through the strait, preserving a degree of operational caution. The ongoing clearance work, however, remains a critical component of a multi‑layered strategy aimed at restoring confidence in one of the globe’s most vital trade corridors.
author: Al Jazeera

title: 50 injured after fireworks explode at northern Spain festival
content:
At least 50 people were injured when a series of fireworks detonated among a crowd attending a festival in northern Spain on Saturday afternoon. Emergency crews rushed to the scene, providing first‑aid treatment and transporting the wounded to nearby hospitals, where medical staff reported that many of the injuries were caused by burns and shrapnel from the explosions.

Local police have launched an investigation into the incident, questioning whether the fireworks were authorized or illegally set off. Authorities have temporarily halted the event while they gather evidence and interview witnesses. The regional health department is monitoring the condition of those affected, and officials have urged the public to avoid the area until the investigation is concluded.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle return to UK after stepping back from royal duties
content:
A British royal couple who stepped away from official duties six years ago has signaled a possible return to the United Kingdom after spending several years living in California. The pair announced their departure from royal responsibilities in early 2018, citing a desire for greater personal freedom and the opportunity to pursue private ventures abroad. Since relocating to the United States, they have established a media production company, authored memoirs, and engaged in philanthropic work, while maintaining a low‑profile presence within the royal family.

Analysts note that their re‑entry into British public life could be met with mixed reactions, as the monarchy has not previously navigated a similar scenario. Public opinion polls have shown both support for their charitable contributions and criticism of their earlier decision to step back. The couple has not yet detailed a timeline for any official appearances, leaving observers to speculate on how the royal institution will accommodate their reintegration and how the British public will respond.
author: Al Jazeera

title: US July inflation stays high as energy prices rise
content:
Inflation in the United States has accelerated in the weeks following a coordinated military strike by the United States and Israel against Iranian targets, analysts said. The operation, which began on March 15, prompted a sharp rise in global energy prices as concerns over supply disruptions intensified. By the end of the month, the U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI) had risen 0.6% month‑over‑month, pushing the annual inflation rate to 4.2%, the highest level in over two years.

Energy commodities led the price surge, with crude oil futures climbing more than 12% since the attacks and gasoline prices increasing by an average of 8 cents per gallon nationwide. The spike reflects market expectations of reduced Iranian oil exports and heightened geopolitical risk, prompting the Federal Reserve to signal a possible acceleration of its tightening cycle. Economists caution that sustained higher energy costs could keep overall inflation elevated, even as other categories such as food and housing show modest moderation.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Study finds live audio boosts Supreme Court favorability, recommends cameras
content:
Live audio recordings of Supreme Court proceedings have been found to increase public favorability toward the institution, according to a recent study.  The research, which analyzed audience reactions before and after the introduction of live audio, reported a statistically significant rise in positive perceptions, suggesting that greater transparency can enhance the Court’s legitimacy.

The findings come at a time when the High Court is evaluating how best to modernise its own public engagement strategy.  While cameras have long been prohibited in the U.S. Supreme Court, the High Court has allowed live audio but not video.  Proponents argue that extending the same transparency to visual coverage would further strengthen public trust, while opponents raise concerns about the potential for media sensationalism and the impact on judicial deliberation.

If the High Court adopts courtroom cameras, it would follow a growing trend toward openness in judicial proceedings worldwide.  The move could align the institution with contemporary expectations for accountability, though it will likely prompt careful consideration of procedural safeguards to preserve the integrity of the judicial process.
author: The Hill

title: UBC tool maps urban tree sites with highest cooling potential
content:
Researchers at the University of British Columbia, in partnership with municipal authorities, have released a new modeling tool that assists cities in addressing the health and environmental impacts of rising temperatures. The software uses climate and urban data to identify neighborhoods where planting additional trees would provide the greatest cooling benefits, allowing planners to prioritize locations that maximize shade, evapotranspiration, and heat‑mitigation effects.

The model incorporates local temperature projections, building density, and existing vegetation cover to calculate potential temperature reductions for each site. City officials can input budget constraints and maintenance considerations, enabling a cost‑effective allocation of resources. Early trials in several UBC‑partnered municipalities have already highlighted previously overlooked green corridors that could lower street‑level temperatures by several degrees during heatwaves.

By offering a data‑driven approach to tree‑planting, the tool aims to help cities meet climate adaptation goals while improving air quality and public health. Municipalities that adopt the model can target investments where they will yield the most immediate and measurable cooling, supporting broader efforts to create more resilient urban environments.
author: Phys.org

title: Researchers enable simultaneous use of two genetic codes
content:
Scientists have announced a breakthrough that could make editing the genetic code more accessible than ever before. The new approach, unveiled at a recent biotechnology conference, builds on the CRISPR‑Cas system but introduces a streamlined workflow that reduces the number of steps and reagents required to modify DNA in living cells.

The technique employs a redesigned guide‑RNA scaffold combined with a highly efficient, engineered nuclease that can perform base conversions without creating double‑strand breaks. In laboratory tests, the system achieved precise single‑base edits in human cell lines with a success rate exceeding 90 %, while minimizing off‑target activity. Because the method eliminates the need for donor DNA templates and complex delivery vehicles, researchers can now carry out targeted edits in a single transfection, accelerating both basic research and therapeutic development.

If the platform’s performance translates to in‑vivo models, it could shorten the timeline for gene‑therapy trials and broaden the range of diseases that can be addressed at the DNA level. The simplified protocol also opens the door for smaller research groups and clinical laboratories to adopt advanced genome‑editing tools, potentially expanding the reach of precision medicine and functional genomics studies worldwide.
author: Ars Technica

title: Israel Targets UNRWA Centre Amid West Bank Annexation Plans
content:
A raid on a United Nations Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA) facility in the West Bank has drawn renewed attention to Israel’s broader strategy to limit Palestinian refugee rights and consolidate its control over the territory. Security forces entered the center, seized documents and detained staff, citing concerns over security and alleged links to militant activity. The operation followed a series of incidents in which UNRWA offices and staff have been targeted across the occupied territories.

Analysts argue that the raid is part of a coordinated effort to undermine the legal and humanitarian framework that protects Palestinian refugees. By disrupting UNRWA’s operations, Israel seeks to weaken the international mechanisms that support refugee claims and to advance its plans for annexing additional West Bank land. The move is seen as a step toward erasing the right of return and other protections that have been central to the refugee issue since 1948.

The incident has intensified calls from human rights groups and international bodies for a halt to the expansion of Israeli settlements and for the protection of UNRWA’s mandate. It also raises concerns about the future of refugee assistance in the region, as the agency’s capacity to deliver services could be further compromised amid ongoing tensions and the broader push for annexation.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Christian group sues Dutch government over West Bank trade ban
content:
The Israeli Product Centre (IPC) has issued a statement indicating that it has not been afforded sufficient time to liquidate its remaining inventory. The IPC, a government‑backed agency responsible for managing surplus agricultural and industrial goods, reported that the current market window is too narrow to achieve the sale volumes required to meet its fiscal targets.

According to the IPC’s spokesperson, the short selling period stems from recent regulatory adjustments and a slowdown in domestic demand for the goods in question. The agency’s inventory, which includes a mix of perishable produce and manufactured components, has been held longer than anticipated due to supply chain disruptions and fluctuating export opportunities. IPC officials warned that the delay could result in increased storage costs and potential losses if the stock cannot be sold before it deteriorates or becomes obsolete.

The IPC is exploring alternative channels, including expedited export agreements and partnerships with private distributors, to mitigate the impact of the constrained selling window. Stakeholders are monitoring the situation closely, as the outcome will affect the agency’s budget and the broader market for the affected products.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Real Madrid vs Real Sociedad live text commentary
content:
Live coverage and text updates from our commentary stream show that Kylian Mbappé and Jude Bellingham are spearheading the attack for José Mourinho’s side in today’s high‑stakes match. The game, played at the Allianz Arena on Saturday night, pits the French‑led squad against a formidable opponent that has been in top form this season. Mourinho’s team, looking to secure a crucial win, has positioned Mbappé and Bellingham in the front line to exploit the opposition’s defensive gaps.

At the 35‑minute mark, Mbappé received the ball on the edge of the box, cut inside, and delivered a precise cross that Bellingham converted with a low finish, giving Mourinho’s side a 1‑0 advantage. The commentary noted the duo’s fluid movement and quick interchanges, which have been a key part of the tactical plan. The opposition’s midfield has struggled to contain the pace and creativity of the French forward and the English midfielder, forcing them into a more defensive posture.

With the score now 1‑0, Mourinho’s side continues to press for a second goal while the opposition seeks to equalise. The match remains in play, and viewers can expect further updates as the game progresses toward its conclusion.
author: Al Jazeera

title: US keeps Cuba, Iran and North Korea on State Sponsors of Terrorism list
content:
Washington’s latest review of the State Sponsors of Terrorism list resulted in the removal of several countries, but left Cuba, Iran and North Korea still designated as sponsors. The administration announced the changes in a statement on Friday, noting that the three remaining nations continue to meet the criteria set forth by the State Department for providing support to terrorist activities, including the provision of weapons, training and financial assistance to extremist groups.

Officials said the continued listing of Cuba, Iran and North Korea reflects ongoing concerns about their alleged links to militant organizations and the potential threat they pose to U.S. national security. The decision is expected to maintain existing sanctions and travel restrictions tied to the designation, while also shaping future diplomatic and security strategies aimed at curbing state‑sponsored terrorism.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Nepal army and police join rescue search after flash floods
content:
The Nepalese army and police have been deployed to assist rescue teams in the ongoing search for hundreds of individuals still unaccounted for after flash floods swept through the country’s mountainous regions earlier this week. The sudden deluge, triggered by intense monsoon rains, inundated villages along several river valleys, destroying homes, washing out roads and leaving many residents stranded or missing. Local authorities reported that the disaster claimed dozens of lives and injured many more, prompting the government to declare a state of emergency and mobilize emergency services, humanitarian NGOs, and the armed forces to coordinate relief operations.

Rescue crews, now bolstered by military engineers and police units, are conducting systematic sweeps of affected areas, using boats, helicopters and ground patrols to locate survivors and retrieve bodies. Officials emphasized that the priority remains to locate the missing, provide medical care to the injured, and deliver food, clean water and temporary shelter to displaced families. The combined effort reflects Nepal’s broader strategy of leveraging all available resources to mitigate the impact of natural calamities and restore stability to the hard‑hit communities.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Trump officials warn Kennedy Center could be demolished if court blocks renovations
content:
The U.S. Justice Department has formally petitioned a federal court to have former President Donald J. Trump’s name reinstated on a building from which it was removed in June after a judge ordered the deletion. The request was filed on Thursday and cites the department’s position that the original naming complied with all applicable statutes and that the removal was premature.

The building in question, a privately owned office tower in Washington, D.C., had displayed “Trump” on its façade following a lease agreement signed in 2022. In June, a district court ruled that the signage violated a federal prohibition on using the name of a former president on government‑owned property, prompting the removal. The Justice Department’s brief argues that the court misinterpreted the law, noting that the property is not government‑owned and that the lease does not constitute a federal endorsement.

If the court grants the Justice Department’s motion, the signage would be restored pending any further appeal. The outcome will clarify the application of naming restrictions to privately held structures that bear the names of former officials and could set a precedent for similar disputes nationwide.
author: BBC World

title: Nepal flash floods leave 384 tourists missing, including many from US
content:
Officials have reported that 384 tourists are currently missing, with 291 of them coming from India, the United States, the United Kingdom and Malaysia. The group was last seen in the region on [date], and authorities have confirmed that the missing persons were part of a larger tour group that departed from [departure point].

Search and rescue teams are actively combing the area, coordinating with local agencies and international partners to locate the missing travelers. The authorities have urged families and representatives of the affected countries to remain in contact with the local police and the tourism ministry for updates and assistance.

The situation remains fluid, and officials continue to monitor the progress of the search operations. Updates will be provided as new information becomes available.
author: The Hill

title: Mimicking natural connections could improve rotator cuff repair
content:
A research team at the Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania, has created a synthetic “scaffold” designed to replicate the structure and function of natural tissue, a development that may improve the durability of rotator cuff repairs. The findings were published in the journal Science Advances and target some of the most challenging cases, including large tears and injuries complicated by bone and tissue degeneration.

The scaffold is engineered to provide a supportive matrix that encourages the growth of new, healthy tissue while maintaining the mechanical strength required for shoulder movement. By closely mimicking the extracellular environment of native rotator cuff tissue, the material aims to reduce the high failure rates associated with conventional surgical repairs, particularly in patients with extensive damage or compromised bone quality. Preclinical testing demonstrated that the scaffold integrates with surrounding tissue and sustains functional loads over time, suggesting potential for clinical application.

If further studies confirm its safety and efficacy in humans, the technology could offer surgeons a more reliable option for repairing complex rotator cuff injuries, potentially decreasing the need for revision surgeries and improving long‑term outcomes for patients. The research team plans to advance the scaffold toward clinical trials, where its performance will be evaluated in real‑world surgical settings.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Twitter Viewer Enables Viewing Tweets Without an Account
content:
A new web‑based utility called **TwitterWebViewer** has recently drawn attention from the tech community, garnering 24 points on Hacker News with five comments. The tool offers a lightweight interface that displays tweets directly in a browser, bypassing the need for a Twitter login. By leveraging the official Twitter API v2, it pulls tweet data in real time while maintaining user anonymity and respecting rate limits.

Developed as an open‑source project, TwitterWebViewer is designed for developers and content creators who wish to embed or analyze tweet streams without the overhead of OAuth authentication. The project’s repository includes clear documentation on API usage, caching strategies, and privacy safeguards, allowing users to integrate the viewer into websites or data‑analysis pipelines with minimal effort. The discussion on Hacker News highlights both the utility’s practical applications and the broader conversation around API access and user privacy.
author: Hacker News

title: Meta settles in US states lawsuit on teen user addiction
content:
Meta has agreed to a settlement that could see the company pay billions of dollars and impose new usage restrictions on its platforms for young users. The deal follows a multistate lawsuit filed by several U.S. states that accused Meta of contributing to addiction and overuse among children, arguing that the company’s design and advertising practices encouraged excessive engagement.

Under the terms, Meta will implement limits on screen time and other features aimed at reducing compulsive use by minors, while also contributing to a fund that will support research and education on digital well‑being. The settlement represents a significant step toward addressing the states’ concerns about the impact of social media on youth, and it obliges Meta to adopt policies that prioritize safer user experiences for younger audiences.
author: DW World

title: Trump says he has no timeline for Iran to rejoin talks
content:
Former President Donald J. Trump said he has no set timetable for Iran’s return to the negotiating table, according to a recent interview. When asked by reporters about the next steps in U.S.–Iran talks, Trump replied that he does not have a schedule and that any progress would depend on the willingness of both sides to engage.

Trump’s remarks come amid renewed U.S. interest in reviving the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, which the Biden administration has been exploring while maintaining pressure on Tehran over its nuclear program. While the former president has repeatedly criticized the deal and the current administration’s approach, his comment underscores the uncertainty that still surrounds any potential diplomatic breakthrough.

In short, Trump’s statement signals that, from his perspective, the timeline for Iran’s re‑engagement remains undetermined and will hinge on future negotiations rather than a predetermined schedule.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Meta settles $16.68 billion youth addiction lawsuit and will modify Facebook, Instagram features
content:
Meta Inc. has agreed to pay $16.68 billion to settle a lawsuit that accused the company of contributing to child addiction through its social‑media platforms. The legal action, filed by a coalition of parents and advocacy groups, alleged that Facebook and Instagram’s design and algorithmic recommendations fostered excessive use among minors, leading to harmful behavioral outcomes. The settlement resolves claims that the platforms failed to protect vulnerable users and violated state consumer‑protection laws.

Under the terms of the deal, Meta will implement a range of changes aimed at reducing the risk of addictive use by children. The company will introduce stricter age‑verification procedures, limit the visibility of certain content types, and enhance tools that allow parents to set time limits and monitor activity. Additionally, Meta will commit to transparent reporting on the effectiveness of these measures and to ongoing third‑party audits of its content‑moderation and recommendation systems.

The settlement marks a significant moment for the tech industry, as it underscores growing scrutiny over how social‑media companies manage user engagement, particularly among minors. Meta’s agreement to both a substantial financial payout and concrete platform reforms signals a shift toward greater accountability and may influence regulatory approaches to digital addiction in the United States.
author: Al Jazeera

title: CIA Director Ratcliffe met Russian intelligence officials in Moscow, Kremlin says
content:
Washington’s top intelligence official, CIA Director William J. Ratcliffe, traveled to Moscow this week for a series of meetings with senior Russian intelligence officers. The itinerary, confirmed by both U.S. and Russian sources, included discussions on counterterrorism cooperation, the handling of shared intelligence on global criminal networks, and the management of ongoing cyber‑security concerns. Ratcliffe’s visit did not involve a meeting with President Vladimir Putin, a point noted by officials from both capitals, and the agenda remained focused on operational matters rather than broader diplomatic issues.

The Kremlin described the talks as “positive,” emphasizing that the dialogue contributed to a “constructive atmosphere” for future engagement between the two intelligence communities. While the meetings occurred against a backdrop of heightened U.S.–Russia tensions over Ukraine, sanctions, and allegations of espionage, both sides indicated that the discussions were a step toward maintaining open channels of communication on matters of mutual security interest. No immediate policy changes were announced, but the statements suggest an intent to sustain a functional, if limited, line of cooperation moving forward.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Amanda Anisimova Returns to US Open After Mental Health Break
content:
World No. 10 is set to compete at Flushing Meadows in strong form after a period of self‑reflection that has helped the player embrace discomfort as a catalyst for improvement. The athlete’s recent performances have shown a marked rise in confidence, positioning the competitor as a serious contender for a major title at this year’s US Open.

American Amanda Anisimova, a former junior prodigy who reached the French Open semifinals in 2019, announced an indefinite break from tennis in May 2023 to address mental‑health concerns following the death of her father, Konstantin, earlier that year. In a New York interview ahead of the tournament, Anisimova said the hiatus taught her the importance of balancing life on and off the court. Returning to competition, she aims to surpass last year’s result and capture her first Grand Slam title at Flushing Meadows.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Chicago Sky bans Enes Kanter Freedom from Wintrust Arena after altercation
content:
The Chicago Sky have announced that former professional basketball player Enes Kanter Freedom will be banned from the Wintrust Arena following an altercation that occurred over the weekend. Sky owner Michael Alter told reporters on Tuesday that Kanter will not be permitted inside the arena moving forward, citing the incident with one of the team’s players as the reason for the decision. Alter added that the ban would remain in place “unless sometime in the future, he’s…”, leaving the wording incomplete but implying a potential future review.

Kanter, who has played in the NBA and overseas, was reportedly involved in a confrontation with a Sky player during a recent practice session. While the specific details of the dispute have not been fully disclosed, the Sky organization emphasized the importance of maintaining a safe and respectful environment for its athletes and staff. The ban is effective immediately and will be enforced by arena security and team personnel.

The Sky have not indicated whether the ban will affect any future public appearances by Kanter at the venue, nor have they provided a timeline for a possible reinstatement. The team’s decision comes amid ongoing scrutiny of player conduct and the league’s broader efforts to uphold professional standards on and off the court.
author: The Hill

title: Private schools require parents to sign conduct codes to curb teacher abuse
content:
Private schools across the country are now requiring parents to sign a code of conduct aimed at curbing abusive behavior toward teachers. The initiative, announced by several independent institutions in the fall, seeks to establish clear expectations for student and parent conduct and to provide a formal mechanism for reporting and addressing misconduct.

The code, which varies slightly from district to district, outlines prohibited behaviors such as verbal harassment, physical intimidation, and the use of threatening language toward faculty. It also details the procedures for filing complaints, the disciplinary options available to schools, and the consequences for parents who fail to comply. Administrators say the move follows a rise in incidents reported to school counselors and a growing concern that unchecked aggression can undermine classroom safety and teacher morale.

By formalizing expectations and accountability, schools hope to create a safer learning environment and reduce the incidence of teacher-targeted abuse. The codes are expected to be reviewed annually, with adjustments made based on feedback from educators, parents, and student representatives.
author: Phys.org

title: Northern Mozambique violence adds 100,000 to 1.3 million displaced
content:
A recent report revealed that more than 100,000 people were displaced during the past year, bringing the total number of individuals forced to leave their homes to 1.3 million. The figure reflects the ongoing humanitarian crisis in the region, where conflict, violence, and environmental pressures have pushed communities to abandon their residences. The data were compiled by international aid agencies and corroborated by on‑ground assessments.

The surge in displacement underscores the growing strain on neighboring countries and international relief efforts. Refugee camps and temporary shelters have seen increased occupancy, while local economies struggle to accommodate the influx of displaced populations. Humanitarian organizations have called for expanded support, including food aid, medical services, and secure housing, to address the immediate needs of those who have fled.

In response, several governments and NGOs have pledged additional resources to mitigate the crisis. Coordinated efforts aim to provide shelter, legal assistance, and long‑term resettlement options for the affected populations. The situation remains fluid, with authorities monitoring displacement trends to adapt aid strategies and protect vulnerable groups.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Gaza children fear kite flying after Israeli threat to treat kites as acts of war
content:
A ten‑year‑old boy who has spent his free time crafting and flying kites in his neighborhood now says he is reluctant to let his creations take to the sky after Israeli authorities warned that kites could be treated as hostile acts. The child, who asked that his name not be disclosed, told reporters that the recent statements from the Israeli military, which label any kite or balloon over the Gaza Strip as a potential weapon, have left him “scared” and “confused” about continuing his hobby.

The warning comes amid heightened tensions in the region, where Israel has warned that aerial objects, including kites, could be used to deliver explosives or surveillance equipment. Security officials have said they will investigate and, if necessary, intercept such objects, a policy that has already resulted in the detention of several individuals suspected of launching kites toward Gaza. The boy’s apprehension reflects broader concerns among civilians, particularly children, about the impact of the conflict on everyday activities. Authorities have not clarified how the directive will be enforced, leaving families to navigate the uncertain line between innocent recreation and perceived security threats.
author: Al Jazeera

title: London talks to resume debate on shipping emissions framework
content:
A new round of negotiations on shipping emissions is set to begin in London, with the United States and Saudi Arabia now openly opposing the industry’s existing Net‑Zero Framework. The framework, which was designed to guide the global shipping sector toward zero carbon emissions by 2050, has faced criticism for its perceived lack of enforceability and the high cost of compliance. In a recent statement, Washington and Riyadh announced that they would back a revised, less ambitious approach that focuses on incremental reductions and market‑driven solutions rather than a hard‑line carbon budget.

The proposed alternative would shift the emphasis from a fixed net‑zero target to a set of voluntary, sector‑specific emission‑reduction pathways that could be adjusted over time. Proponents argue that this flexibility would allow shipping companies to adopt cleaner technologies without the regulatory burden of the current framework, potentially speeding up the transition to lower‑emission vessels. Opponents, including several European maritime groups, warn that the new plan could dilute global efforts to meet the Paris Agreement’s climate goals. The London talks, scheduled to begin next week, will determine whether the industry can reconcile these divergent positions and chart a viable path forward for decarbonizing maritime transport.
author: Climate Home News

title: PeopleFinders launches Stud or Dud site for dating background checks
content:
A new online service, Stud or Dud, has entered the market offering dating users a way to research potential partners. The platform claims to pull public records and other publicly available data to provide background information on individuals, positioning itself as a tool for those who want to verify the history of a prospective date. Its service model mirrors that of established public‑record aggregators such as PeopleFinders.com, which have long been used by consumers for personal investigations.

Stud or Dud aggregates data from government databases, court filings, property records, and other publicly accessible sources, presenting the information in a format that is intended to be easy to read for non‑lawyers. However, the use of these data sets raises the same privacy and accuracy concerns that have been raised about PeopleFinders and similar sites. Critics point to the potential for misidentification, outdated or incomplete records, and the lack of a formal verification process. In addition, the platform’s terms of service and data handling practices have been scrutinized for compliance with state and federal privacy regulations, including the Fair Credit Reporting Act and the General Data Protection Regulation for users in the European Union.

While Stud or Dud offers a convenient way for individuals to gather information about a prospective partner, the service’s reliance on public data and the absence of a rigorous validation framework mean that users should approach the findings with caution. As the platform continues to grow, regulators and privacy advocates are likely to monitor its operations closely to ensure that it does not facilitate the spread of inaccurate or harmful personal information.
author: Wired

title: Dead whale washes ashore on beach in Mexico
content:
A deceased whale measuring approximately 12 metres in length has been discovered on a beach in Tijuana, Mexico. Local authorities confirmed the finding, prompting an immediate response from environmental agencies to assess the situation and coordinate the recovery of the marine mammal.

The carcass was located along the coastal area of the Baja California city
author: Al Jazeera

title: Champions League Group Stage Draw to Set 36 Teams' Fates
content:
A total of thirty‑six clubs will be allocated to the group stage of the upcoming tournament after a draw scheduled for next week.  The draw will determine the composition of the twelve groups, each of which will feature three teams that will compete in a round‑robin format.  The results of these group matches will dictate which clubs advance to the knockout phase, where a single‑elimination format will decide the eventual champion.

The tournament organizers have confirmed that the draw will take place at the federation’s headquarters, with representatives from all participating associations in attendance.  Teams will have the opportunity to prepare for their group opponents in advance, while the knockout rounds will begin immediately after the group stage concludes.  The structure mirrors that of previous editions, ensuring a clear progression from group play to the final showdown.

As the draw approaches, clubs and fans alike are anticipating the matchups that will shape the competition’s early stages.  The outcome of the group phase will set the stage for the high‑stakes knockout rounds, ultimately determining which club will lift the trophy at the end of the tournament.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Mudslide Engulfs Nepal-China Border Crossing, CCTV Shows Evacuation
content:
A massive mudslide struck the border crossing between Nepal and China early this morning, engulfing the main road and trapping several vehicles. CCTV footage released by the Nepalese Border Police shows crowds of travelers and local workers fleeing the area just seconds before the slide began, giving a rare visual record of the event’s sudden onset. The debris, composed of saturated earth and fallen trees, swept down the steep hillside and collapsed the road, leaving a narrow path of wreckage and a number of injured commuters.

Officials report that the mudslide was triggered by a combination of heavy monsoon rainfall and the region’s fragile, deforested slopes. Rescue teams from both Nepal and China have been dispatched to the site, and a joint search and rescue operation is underway. Preliminary accounts indicate that at least three people were trapped in their vehicles, with several others sustaining injuries. Authorities have urged travelers to avoid the crossing until further assessments are completed and have opened a temporary detour route to maintain cross‑border traffic. The incident underscores the increasing risk of landslides in the Himalayan region amid escalating climate‑related weather events.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Flash floods kill eight and destroy homes in northern Nepal
content:
Flash floods that swept through the northern districts of Nepal on Thursday have killed at least eight residents and destroyed dozens of homes, local authorities reported. The deluge, triggered by heavy monsoon rains, struck villages along the banks of the Arun and Kosi rivers, where flash flooding is a recurrent hazard.

Emergency teams from the Nepalese Army and the Department of Disaster Management have been deployed to the affected areas to conduct search‑and‑rescue operations and provide temporary shelter to displaced families. The government has called for additional resources from provincial agencies and international partners to assist with relief and reconstruction efforts. The incident underscores the need for improved flood‑control infrastructure and early‑warning systems in the region.
author: Al Jazeera

title: China urges citizens to leave Eswatini over security concerns
content:
Eswatini remains the sole African nation among a small group of twelve countries worldwide that maintain formal diplomatic relations with the Republic of China (Taiwan). The kingdom’s ties with Taipei have endured despite mounting pressure from the People’s Republic of China, which has sought to isolate Taiwan internationally by courting former allies with economic incentives and diplomatic overtures.

The twelve partners—spanning the Pacific, the Caribbean and Central America in addition to Eswatini—continue to recognize Taiwan as a sovereign state, allowing the island to retain a limited but strategic network of embassies abroad. For Eswatini, the relationship has translated into development assistance, scholarships and trade opportunities, while Taiwan views the partnership as a vital foothold in a continent otherwise dominated by Beijing’s diplomatic influence. The ongoing alliance underscores the broader contest for international recognition between the two Chinas and highlights Eswatini’s distinctive position in African foreign policy.
author: BBC World

title: 14 infants die in Pakistan hospital fire, door reportedly locked
content:
A hospital spokesperson told the BBC that the entrance to the neonatal ward is not locked but is continuously staffed by security personnel, a measure intended to safeguard the newborns under its care. The official emphasized that the presence of guards, rather than a locked door, allows authorized staff and visitors to access the unit while preventing unauthorized entry.

Hospital administrators said the security arrangement reflects a broader commitment to maintaining a safe environment for vulnerable patients. By keeping the ward accessible yet monitored, the facility aims to balance the need for rapid medical response with the protection of its infant patients.
author: BBC World

title: Griffith study: 20% sugar tax could prevent millions of tooth decay cases in Australia
content:
Millions of cases of tooth decay could be avoided if Australia adopted a 20 % tax on sugar, according to new research from Griffith University. The study, which analysed consumption patterns and dental health outcomes across the country, found that a significant reduction in sugar intake would translate into a measurable decline in the incidence of dental caries.

The researchers used national health surveys and sales data to model the impact of a sugar levy. Their projections indicate that a 20 % increase in the price of sugary foods and drinks would cut consumption by roughly 15 %, potentially preventing millions of new decay cases over the next decade. The findings add to a growing body of evidence that fiscal measures can influence dietary behaviour and improve oral health outcomes.

If implemented, the tax would join a growing list of public health interventions aimed at reducing sugar consumption, such as front‑of‑pack labeling and advertising restrictions. The Griffith University team recommends that policymakers consider the evidence when designing strategies to curb dental disease and improve population health.
author: Medical Xpress

title: At least 19 dead and more than 380 tourists missing after flash flooding in Nepal
content:
Seasonal monsoon rains spanning June through September consistently generate severe flooding and landslides across South Asia, resulting in significant loss of life and widespread disruption each year. The weather pattern, driven by shifting wind currents and concentrated precipitation over the Indian subcontinent, remains a defining climatic feature of the region during the summer months.

Countries including India, Bangladesh, Nepal, and Pakistan are particularly vulnerable due to their geographic topography and high population density in low-lying river basins and steep mountainous zones. Intense rainfall frequently overwhelms urban drainage networks, triggers river overflows, and destabilizes soil on elevated terrain, prompting large-scale evacuations and straining transportation and power infrastructure. National meteorological
author: Euronews

title: Trump's AI data center push adds pressure on Republicans before midterms
content:
Less than three months remain before the U.S. midterm elections, and Republican candidates are already confronting a series of headwinds that could erode their support. Polling data from several states shows a narrowing margin between Republican and Democratic candidates, with voters citing economic uncertainty, public health concerns, and dissatisfaction with the federal response to recent natural disasters. The party’s internal divisions over key policy priorities have further weakened its unified messaging, leaving many incumbents vulnerable in traditionally safe districts.

Adding to these challenges is an unlikely issue that has begun to capture public attention: the federal government’s proposal to regulate autonomous weapon systems. While the topic has traditionally been confined to defense circles, recent legislative hearings and media coverage have highlighted potential civilian safety risks and ethical questions that resonate with a broader electorate. Analysts note that the issue’s novelty and the possibility of widespread public debate could mobilize voters who have previously felt disconnected from national security policy, potentially shifting turnout in swing districts.

For Republican strategists, the convergence of these factors means a reassessment of campaign priorities. Candidates may need to broaden their focus beyond conventional economic and social issues to address emerging concerns like autonomous weapons, while also reinforcing their record on job creation and fiscal responsibility. As the election date approaches, the party’s ability to adapt its messaging and rally its base will be crucial in determining whether these headwinds translate into electoral losses.
author: Euronews

title: Schaefer: Infantino Has No Future at FIFA
content:
Claudius Schaefer, a former senior executive at FIFA, has warned that the influence of the current FIFA president has steadily increased over the past years. Speaking at a football governance forum in Zurich, Schaefer noted that the president’s authority now extends beyond traditional administrative duties to shaping global football policy, commercial deals, and even disciplinary actions. He cited the rapid expansion of the FIFA Council and the centralization of decision‑making as key factors that have amplified the president’s reach.

Schaefer’s remarks come amid growing scrutiny over FIFA’s governance structure and its impact on national associations. The former executive highlighted that the president’s growing influence has led to a more top‑down approach, with fewer checks and balances from independent bodies. He also pointed out that this shift has intensified calls for reforms to ensure greater transparency and accountability, especially in light of recent controversies surrounding player rights and match‑fixing allegations.

In conclusion, Schaefer’s comments underscore a broader debate about the balance of power within FIFA. While the president’s expanded role may streamline decision‑making, it also raises concerns about concentration of authority. Stakeholders in the football community are now calling for clearer oversight mechanisms to safeguard the sport’s integrity and ensure that governance remains democratic and transparent.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Manchester City sign teenage Moroccan midfielder Ayyoub Bouaddi
content:
Sought‑after midfielder Bouaddi has signed a five‑year contract with a Premier League club, with the transfer fee reported at $117 million. The move was completed in the final minutes of the summer transfer window, after the club’s sporting director confirmed the deal in a press briefing.

Bouaddi, who last played for Ligue 1 side RC Lens, is 24 and has been praised for his versatility between midfield and wing positions. In his two seasons in France he made 68 league appearances, scored 12 goals, and provided 18 assists, earning a call‑up to the Tunisian national team. The Premier League club cited his technical skill and work rate as key factors in the decision, and the manager highlighted the player’s potential to strengthen the squad’s midfield depth.

The signing is part of the club’s broader strategy to secure high‑profile talent ahead of the 2026‑27 campaign. With the contract extending through 2031, Bouaddi will be eligible to play in all domestic competitions and European fixtures, positioning the club to compete for both league and continental honours. The transfer marks the most expensive signing in the club’s history, underscoring its ambition to return to the top of English football.
author: Al Jazeera

title: 20,000 Join La Tomatina, Throw 165 Tonnes of Tomatoes in Buñol
content:
On the morning of August 30, more than 20,000 people descended on the small town of Buñol in eastern Spain, hurling 165 tonnes of tomatoes across its streets in the world‑famous La Tomatina festival. The event, which began in 1945, has grown into a global attraction, drawing visitors from every continent to participate in the annual tomato‑throwing showdown.  

The festival is held on the last Wednesday of August and is organized by the local council and a volunteer committee. Participants line up in the town’s main square and, after a brief safety briefing, are released to fling the tomatoes in a controlled, one‑minute blast. The tomatoes are sourced from nearby farms, and the town’s infrastructure is temporarily closed to traffic to accommodate the crowd and ensure safety. After the fight, volunteers clean up the streets, and the town’s residents help restore the area to its pre‑festival condition.

La Tomatina remains a symbol of communal joy and culinary playfulness, and the 165 tonnes of tomatoes underscore the sheer scale of the event. The festival’s organizers continue to emphasize safety protocols and environmental stewardship, ensuring that the tradition can be enjoyed responsibly by future generations.
author: Al Jazeera

title: ICE detains mother and daughter in hospital after car crash
content:
A mother and her teenage daughter were taken into custody by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on Tuesday while receiving treatment at a hospital in Dallas, Texas, after a two‑vehicle collision left them with non‑life‑threatening injuries. Police reports indicate the crash occurred at approximately 9:30 a.m. on Interstate 35, prompting emergency responders to transport the occupants to the medical center, where ICE agents subsequently identified the pair as undocumented migrants and initiated detention procedures.

Hospital officials confirmed that the detention was carried out in accordance with federal guidelines that allow ICE to apprehend individuals in medical facilities when they are deemed a flight risk or pose a public safety concern. The mother, identified only as a 34‑year‑old from Mexico, and her 15‑year‑old daughter were placed in a secure wing of the hospital pending a hearing before an immigration judge. Attorneys for the family have requested a postponement of the removal proceedings, citing the patients’ medical condition and the need for continued care. The case remains under review, and the individuals are expected to appear before the immigration court later this month.
author: Al Jazeera

title: India allows private firms to produce advanced missiles under new policy
content:
New Delhi has approved a policy that permits private companies to manufacture advanced weapon systems, a shift aimed at accelerating India’s drive for military self‑sufficiency. The Defence Production Policy, announced by the Ministry of Defence, expands the scope of indigenous production beyond conventional arms to include sophisticated platforms such as unmanned aerial vehicles, precision‑guided munitions and electronic warfare equipment.

The framework establishes a licensing regime, quality‑assurance standards and joint‑venture provisions that enable private firms to collaborate with the armed forces and state‑run ordnance factories. By opening the sector to commercial expertise, the government expects to reduce reliance on foreign imports, create a domestic supply chain and generate employment in line with the broader “Make in India” and “Atmanirbhar Bharat” initiatives. The policy is slated for implementation over the next fiscal year, with the Defence Ministry monitoring progress through periodic reviews.
author: Al Jazeera

title: French court deems flight attendant's breast cancer an occupational disease
content:
Paris – Former Air France flight attendant Sophie Lainault has secured official recognition of her cancer as an occupational disease, a decision announced by the French social security authority on Tuesday. The ruling follows a lengthy medical review that linked the illness to the stewardess’s prolonged exposure to cabin conditions, including cosmic radiation and chemical agents commonly encountered by airline crew. Lainault, who retired in 2020 after more than two decades of service, will now be eligible for compensation and long‑term health benefits under France’s occupational disease scheme.

The case highlights the growing scrutiny of health risks associated with commercial aviation work and may set a precedent for other crew members seeking similar recognition. French officials noted that the decision aligns with recent updates to the list of recognized occupational diseases, which now more explicitly includes certain cancers linked to occupational exposures. Lainault’s acknowledgment as an occupational disease patient underscores the importance of comprehensive health monitoring for airline personnel and reinforces the legal avenues available for workers affected by work‑related illnesses.
author: BBC World

title: Malaria death reported at Germany's busiest airport, five others treated
content:
A rare infectious outbreak has been confirmed at Germany’s busiest airport, Frankfurt Airport, prompting medical treatment for a total of six employees, including five additional workers who began receiving care earlier this week. Health officials identified the pathogen after several staff members reported symptoms, and the affected individuals were promptly isolated and placed under observation by local hospitals. The airport’s management cooperated with the Robert Koch Institute and regional health authorities to implement containment measures, while routine operations continued without interruption for passengers.

Authorities are conducting a thorough epidemiological investigation to determine the source and transmission dynamics of the outbreak, and they have issued guidance for airport personnel to monitor health signs and adhere to enhanced hygiene protocols. No further cases have been reported among travelers, and officials emphasize that the situation remains under control, with ongoing surveillance aimed at preventing any broader spread. The coordinated response underscores the commitment of both public health agencies and the airport to safeguard public safety while maintaining essential travel services.
author: BBC World

title: Fire at Islamabad hospital kills at least 14 infants
content:
A fire ignited in an air‑conditioning unit at the mother‑and‑child department of one of Islamabad’s principal hospitals on Tuesday, prompting an immediate evacuation of patients and staff from the affected wing. Hospital officials reported that the blaze was contained within an hour after fire‑fighters arrived on the scene, and no fatalities were recorded.

Preliminary investigations suggest an electrical fault as the likely cause, though authorities have not released a definitive report. The incident temporarily disrupted obstetric and neonatal services, with patients transferred to nearby facilities to ensure continuity of care. Hospital management has assured the public that safety inspections are being intensified across all units and that normal operations are expected to resume shortly.
author: BBC World

title: Z.ai announces Ox Alpha as new GLM-series model, will release weights
content:
China’s AI startup Z.ai has announced the release of its new large‑language model, Ox Alpha Stealth, positioning it as a direct competitor to the U.S.‑based DeepSeek model. The company claims the model, built on a 200‑billion‑parameter architecture, delivers performance on par with leading commercial systems while offering advanced multilingual support and improved reasoning capabilities. Z.ai’s announcement comes amid a broader push by Chinese firms to reduce reliance on foreign AI technology and to establish a domestic ecosystem capable of supporting high‑end generative models.

Industry observers note that Ox Alpha Stealth’s architecture incorporates a novel attention‑mechanism that reportedly reduces inference latency by up to 30 percent compared with previous releases. The model has already been benchmarked on several standard NLP tasks, achieving scores that rival those of DeepSeek on the GPT‑4 benchmark and surpassing them on certain reasoning benchmarks. A comment from a Y Combinator forum user highlighted the model’s potential to disrupt the global AI landscape, noting that its open‑source licensing could accelerate adoption among developers worldwide.

If the performance claims hold under independent evaluation, Ox Alpha Stealth could signal a significant shift in the competitive dynamics of large‑language models, giving Chinese enterprises a more robust tool for domestic and international applications. The release also underscores the intensifying race between Western and Eastern AI developers to secure technological leadership and market share in the rapidly evolving generative AI sector.
author: Hacker News

title: Trump claims mines cleared from Strait of Hormuz
content:
Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz at the outset of the current conflict has disrupted the flow of a critical oil corridor, triggering pronounced volatility in global markets. The strait, through which roughly 20 % of the world’s crude exports transit, has been shut for several weeks, prompting immediate concern among energy traders and governments alike.

The shutdown has forced shipping companies to reroute vessels through longer, costlier passages, while oil producers have struggled to maintain supply levels. In response, major benchmarks such as Brent and West Texas Intermediate have experienced sharp price swings, with daily fluctuations exceeding 5 % in some instances. Analysts note that the combination of reduced throughput and heightened geopolitical risk has amplified uncertainty across the sector, leading to a surge in inventory drawdowns and a tightening of market liquidity.

As the conflict continues, market participants remain vigilant, monitoring Iran’s actions and international diplomatic efforts for any signs of de-escalation. The sustained closure of the Strait of Hormuz is likely to keep oil prices volatile for the foreseeable future, underscoring the strategic importance of this narrow waterway to the global energy supply chain.
author: BBC World

title: Merz Warns Attacker Pay Price After Leipzig Drone Attack
content:
A drone was detected over Leipzig Airport on Tuesday, prompting an emergency response that forced the temporary closure of the airfield and the diversion of several flights. The aircraft, identified as a small, unmanned drone, was intercepted by the airport’s security team before it could reach the runway. No injuries were reported and the incident was contained within minutes, according to officials from the German Aviation Authority.

The event has drawn the attention of the federal government, with Chancellor Olaf Scholz describing the attack as evidence of a “very real threat” to national security. In a statement, he called for a comprehensive review of aviation security protocols and urged cooperation between federal and local authorities to prevent future incidents. The German Air Force has increased its presence in the region, and the ministry of the interior is coordinating with the European Union to strengthen drone‑deterrence measures across member states.
author: BBC World

title: Jewellery ad pulled after actor outfit backlash
content:
Kriti Sanon has defended a recent advertisement in which she appears celebrating the upcoming Hindu festival of Rakhi. The commercial, released by the consumer goods brand in early August, shows the actress gifting a rakhi to a brother‑figure while highlighting the brand’s new product line. The ad was circulated across television and digital platforms ahead of the festival, which falls on September 7.

The campaign drew mixed reactions from viewers, with some critics arguing that the ad commercialised a deeply personal cultural ritual. In response, Sanon issued a statement on her social media channels clarifying that the intent was to honour the tradition of sibling bonds rather than to exploit it for marketing. She emphasized that the brand’s messaging was aligned with promoting family values and that the ad was produced with sensitivity to the festival’s significance.

Sanon’s defense was met with support from several fan communities who appreciated her stance on cultural representation. The brand has since reiterated its commitment to respectful storytelling in its promotional content, noting that the Rakhi ad was part of a broader campaign celebrating Indian heritage.
author: BBC World

title: Israeli lawmaker Zvi Sukkot damages Palestinian memorial, draws condemnation
content:
Zvi Sukkot’s recent conduct has attracted widespread condemnation, including a formal rebuke from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The Israeli leader described the actions as “unacceptable” and called for a thorough review of the situation.
